C.3 Derivation of the ∇\nablasmc gradient estimator [Eq. 24]

We derive the ∇\nablasmc estimator of the gradient ℱ=𝔼(x,y)∼π​[A⁡(x,y)]\mathcal{F}=\mathbb{E}_{(x,y)\sim\pi}[A(x,y)] in Eq. 24 and show that it admits the form ∇ℱ=𝑿⊤​𝜺\gradient\mathcal{F}=\bm{X}^{\top}\bm{\varepsilon}.

One straightforward approach is to reverse the marginalization yielding the ∇\nablacmc gradient estimator [Eq. 25]

∇θℱ\displaystyle\gradient_{\theta}\mathcal{F} =𝔼πψ[2Re⁡{Δ​J​(x)∗​Hloc​(x)}]=2Re{∑xπψ(x)ΔJ∗(x)Hloc(x)}\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\psi}}[2\Re{\Delta J(x)^{*} H_{\rm loc}(x)}]=2\real\{\sum_{x}\pi_{\psi}(x)\Delta J^{*}(x)H_{\rm loc}(x)\Big\} (70)
=2Re{∑xπψ(x)ΔJ(x)∗ϕ⁡(x)ψ⁡(x)∑yπϕ(y)ψ⁡(y)ϕ⁡(x)}=𝔼z∼π[2Re⁡{Δ​J​(x)​A​(z)∗}]\displaystyle=2\real\{\sum_{x}\pi_{\psi}(x)\Delta J(x)^{*}\frac{\phi(x)}{\psi(x)}\sum_{y}\pi_{\phi}(y)\frac{\psi(y)}{\phi(x)}\Big\}=\mathbb{E}_{z\sim\pi}[2\Re{\Delta J(x) A(z)^{*}}]
=𝔼z∼π​[(Δ​Jre​(x)Δ​Jim​(x))⋅(2​Re⁡{A⁡(z)}2​Im⁡{A⁡(z)})].\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{z\sim\pi}\quantity[\left(\begin{array}{c} \Delta J^{\rm re}(x) \\[0.2em] \Delta J^{\rm im}(x) \end{array}\right) \cdot\left(\begin{array}{c} 2\Re{A(z)} \\[0.2em] 2\Im{A(z)} \end{array}\right)].

In practice, the expectation value above is evaluated using MC sampling as

∇ℱ≈1Ns​∑i=1NsΔ​Jre​(xi)​Re⁡{A⁡(xi,yi)}+Δ​Jim​(xi)​Im⁡{A⁡(xi,yi)},\gradient\mathcal{F}\approx\frac{1}{N_{s}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{s}}\Delta J^{\rm re}(x_{i})\Re{A(x_i,y_i)}+\Delta J^{\rm im}(x_{i})\Im{A(x_i,y_i)}, (71)

which makes manifest the possibility of expressing the gradient as ∇ℱ=𝑿​ε\gradient\mathcal{F}=\bm{X}\varepsilon with

𝒇=2Ns​(A⁡(x1,y1),…,A⁡(xNs,yNs))∈ℂNs,\bm{f}=\frac{2}{\sqrt{N_{s}}}\Big(A(x_{1},y_{1}),\ldots,A(x_{N_{s}},y_{N_{s}})\Big)\in\mathbb{C}^{N_{s}}, (72)

and

𝜺=(Re⁡{𝒇}Im⁡{𝒇})∈ℝ2​Ns.\bm{\varepsilon}=\begin{pmatrix}\Re{\bm f}\\[2.15277pt] \Im{\bm f}\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{2N_{s}}. (73)

Although this derivation would suffice, it is still insightful to explore how the same expression can be obtained by manipulating the ∇\nablacv-smc estimator [Eq. 26, or equivalently Eq. 69]. The value in this alternative derivation stems from the properties of A⁡(z)A(z) that this approach reveals. We believe these properties could be useful in the future to derive control variables tailored to the gradient. For starters, we find that

𝔼z∼π​[|A⁡(z)|2​f​(x)]=𝔼y∼πϕ​[f⁡(y)].\mathbb{E}_{z\sim\pi}\quantity[\abs{A(z)}^2 f(x)]=\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\phi}}\quantity[f(y)]. (74)

Using this identity, one can easily show that

𝔼z∼π​[A∗​(z)​f​(x)]=𝔼z∼π​[A⁡(z)​f​(y)],\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{z\sim\pi}\quantity[A^*(z) f(x)]=\mathbb{E}_{z\sim\pi}\quantity[A(z) f(y)], (75)
𝔼z∼π​[A∗​(z)​f​(y)]=𝔼z∼π​[A⁡(z)​f​(x)],\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{z\sim\pi}\quantity[A^*(z) f(y)]=\mathbb{E}_{z\sim\pi}\quantity[A(z) f(x)], (76)
𝔼z∼π​[A⁡(z)​f​(x)]=𝔼z∼π​[A∗​(z)​f​(y)],\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{z\sim\pi}\quantity[A(z) f(x)]=\mathbb{E}_{z\sim\pi}\quantity[A^*(z) f(y)], (77)
𝔼z∼π​[A⁡(z)​f​(y)]=𝔼z∼π​[A∗​(z)​f​(x)].\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{z\sim\pi}\quantity[A(z) f(y)]=\mathbb{E}_{z\sim\pi}\quantity[A^*(z) f(x)]. (78)

Again, these equations can be combined to show that

𝔼z∼π​[f⁡(x)​Re⁡{A⁡(z)}]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{z\sim\pi}\quantity[f(x) \Re{A(z)}] =𝔼z∼π​[f⁡(y)​Re⁡{A⁡(z)}],\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{z\sim\pi}\quantity[f(y) \Re{A(z)}], (79)
𝔼z∼π​[f⁡(x)​Im⁡{A⁡(z)}]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{z\sim\pi}\quantity[f(x) \Im{A(z)}] =−𝔼z∼π​[f⁡(y)​Im⁡{A⁡(z)}].\displaystyle=-\mathbb{E}_{z\sim\pi}\quantity[f(y) \Im{A(z)}]. (80)

Substitution into Eq. 69 yields Eq. 70.

Appendix D Covariance structure, Rao-Blackwellization, and variance reduction

We use this appendix to expand on the differences in variance exhibited by the gradient estimators presented in the main text. First off, we note that while both the ∇\nablacmc and ∇\nablasmc estimators take the form of a covariance estimator [c.f. Eqs. 60 and 70], the ∇\nablacv-smc estimator does not. Generally, estimators structured as covariances tend to exhibit lower variance largely due to the inherent variance reduction from centering each component. Specifically, the sample covariance used to estimate the covariance between two random variables XX and YY is given by

Cov⁡(X,Y)=𝔼⁡[(X−𝔼⁡[X])​(Y−𝔼⁡[Y])]≈γNs​∑i=1Ns(Xi−1Ns​∑j=1NsXj)​(Yi−1Ns​∑j=1NsYj),\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=\mathbb{E}[(X-\mathbb{E}[X])(Y-\mathbb{E}[Y])]\approx\frac{\gamma}{N_{s}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{s}}\left(X_{i}-\frac{1}{N_{s}}\sum_{j=1}^{N_{s}}X_{j}\right)\left(Y_{i}-\frac{1}{N_{s}}\sum_{j=1}^{N_{s}}Y_{j}\right), (81)

where γ=Ns/(Ns−1)\gamma=N_{s}/(N_{s}-1) is the Bessel correction factor used to remove the bias introduced by centering. The centering process effectively provides sample-specific control variates that automatically adjust to the non-stationarity of the variables, enhancing estimator stability, and justifying the results presented in the main text and further corroborated by Fig. 9.

While the poor performance of the ∇\nablacv-smc estimator is attributed to its lack of a covariance structure, the smaller performance difference between the ∇\nablacmc and ∇\nablasmc estimators can be understood through the Rao-Blackwell theorem. Identical arguments apply for the cmc and smc estimators of the fidelity itself. In the simplest setting, Rao-Blackwellization replaces a function of two random variables with its conditional expectation resulting in a new estimator whose variance is no greater than that of the original function (Rao-Blackwell theorem). Consider two random variables, XX and YY, and a function J⁡(X,Y)J(X,Y). Our goal is to compute its expectation 𝔼⁡[J⁡(X,Y)]\mathbb{E}[J(X,Y)] with respect to the joint distribution of XX and YY. To do so, we define [74]

𝔼⁡[J⁡(X,Y)∣X]=∑yJ⁡(x,y)⋅P⁡(Y=y∣X=x)≡J^​(X)\mathbb{E}[J(X,Y)\mid X]=\sum_{y}J(x,y)\cdot P(Y=y\mid X=x)\equiv\hat{J}(X) (82)

and note that 𝔼⁡[J^​(X)]=𝔼⁡[J⁡(X,Y)]\mathbb{E}[\hat{J}(X)]=\mathbb{E}[J(X,Y)]. This implies that J^​(X)\hat{J}(X) can be used in place of J⁡(X,Y)J(X,Y) in a Monte Carlo approximation of 𝔼⁡[J⁡(X,Y)]\mathbb{E}[J(X,Y)]. The variance of J^​(X)\hat{J}(X) can be easily computed to be

Var​(J^​(X))=Var​(J⁡(X,Y))−𝔼⁡[(J⁡(X,Y)−J^​(X))2],\text{Var}(\hat{J}(X))=\text{Var}(J(X,Y))-\mathbb{E}[(J(X,Y)-\hat{J}(X))^{2}], (83)

from which it follows that Var​(J^​(X))≤Var​(J⁡(X,Y))\text{Var}(\hat{J}(X))\leq\text{Var}(J(X,Y)). To compute Rao-Blackwellized estimators, we generally need to calculate conditional expectations. In many cases, this cannot be done exactly; however, under a mean-field assumption, the conditional expectation simplifies due to factorization:

J^​(X)=𝔼⁡[J⁡(X,Y)∣X]=∑yJ⁡(x,y)⋅P⁡(Y=y∣X=x)=∑yJ⁡(x,y)⋅P⁡(Y=y)=𝔼Y​[J⁡(X,Y)],\hat{J}(X)=\mathbb{E}[J(X,Y)\mid X]=\sum_{y}J(x,y)\cdot P(Y=y\mid X=x)=\sum_{y}J(x,y)\cdot P(Y=y)=\mathbb{E}_{Y}[J(X,Y)], (84)

where we used that P⁡(X,Y)=P⁡(X)​P​(Y)P(X,Y)=P(X)P(Y) and thus P⁡(Y∣X)=P⁡(Y)P(Y\mid X)=P(Y). Therefore, to construct a lower variance estimator when the joint distribution factorizes, all we need to do is integrate out some variables and use this marginal as the estimator.

Appendix E Lowering sampling cost by reweighting

Direct evaluation of the fidelity (and of its gradient) between two transformed states |ψ~⟩=V^​|ψ⟩\ket*{\tilde\psi}=\hat{V}\ket*{\psi} and |ϕ~⟩=U^​|ϕ⟩\ket*{\tilde\phi}=\hat{U}\ket*{\phi} requires, in principle, sampling from their Born distributions πψ~​(x)\pi_{\tilde{\psi}}(x) and πϕ~​(y)\pi_{\tilde{\phi}}(y), respectively. This process introduces a computational overhead that scales with NcN_{c}, the number of connected elements in the transformations. For local spin Hamiltonians, this introduces a sampling overhead proportional to the system size NN, which often becomes the dominant cost (in the simulations presented in Section 4, for instance, around 90% of the computational time is spent sampling). The computational burden grows substantially for other Hamiltonians, such as for those arising in natural-orbital chemistry or for the kinetic term in first-quantisation formulations [109].

To address this overhead, one can resort to self-normalized importance sampling [73], adapting the estimators discussed in Section 3 to sample directly from the bare distributions. In line with the procedure outlined in Ref. [47], we avoid direct sampling from the target state. While previous works were concerned with unitary transformations applied to the target state alone, here we extend the approach to arbitrary transformations that act on both the target and variational states.

As all estimators discussed in Section 3 are of this form, it is convenient to write down the reweighting procedure just once for the generic estimator 𝔼σ∼χ​[f​(σ)]\mathbb{E}_{\sigma\sim\chi}[f(\sigma)]. In this case, we have [73]

𝔼σ∼χ​[f⁡(σ)]=𝔼σ∼η​[w⁡(σ)​f​(σ)]𝔼σ∼η​[w​(σ)],\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\sigma\sim\chi}[f(\sigma)]=\frac{\mathbb{E}_{\sigma\sim\eta}[w(\sigma)f(\sigma)]}{\mathbb{E}_{\sigma\sim\eta}[w(\sigma)]}, (85)

where w=η/χw=\eta/\chi. Specializing to the case where we sample from a joint distribution, e.g. in Eqs. 18, 20, 24 and 26, yields

𝔼(x,y)∼π~​[f⁡(x,y)]=∑x,yπ⁡(x,y)​π~​(x,y)π⁡(x,y)​f​(x,y)∑x,yπ⁡(x,y)​π~​(x,y)π⁡(x,y),\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{(x,y)\sim\tilde{\pi}}[f(x,y)]=\frac{\sum_{x,y}\pi(x,y)\frac{\tilde{\pi}(x,y)}{\pi(x,y)}f(x,y)}{\sum_{x,y}\pi(x,y)\frac{\tilde{\pi}(x,y)}{\pi(x,y)}}, (86)

where π~​(x,y)=πψ~​(x)​πϕ~​(y)\tilde{\pi}(x,y)=\pi_{\tilde{\psi}}(x)\pi_{\tilde{\phi}}(y). Applying Rao-Blackwellization to this estimator is still possible and results in

𝔼(x,y)∼π~​[f⁡(x,y)]=𝔼x∼π~ψ​[fx​(x)]​𝔼y∼π~ϕ​[fy​(y)]=∑xπψ​(x)​π~ψ​(x)πψ​(x)​fx​(x)∑xπψ​(x)​π~ψ​(x)πψ​(x)​∑yπϕ​(y)​π~ϕ​(y)πϕ​(y)​fy​(y)∑yπϕ​(y)​π~ϕ​(y)πϕ​(y),\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{(x,y)\sim\tilde{\pi}}[f(x,y)]=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\tilde{\pi}_{\psi}}[f_{x}(x)]\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\tilde{\pi}_{\phi}}[f_{y}(y)]=\frac{\sum_{x}\pi_{\psi}(x)\frac{\tilde{\pi}_{\psi}(x)}{\pi_{\psi}(x)}f_{x}(x)}{\sum_{x}\pi_{\psi}(x)\frac{\tilde{\pi}_{\psi}(x)}{\pi_{\psi}(x)}}\frac{\sum_{y}\pi_{\phi}(y)\frac{\tilde{\pi}_{\phi}(y)}{\pi_{\phi}(y)}f_{y}(y)}{\sum_{y}\pi_{\phi}(y)\frac{\tilde{\pi}_{\phi}(y)}{\pi_{\phi}(y)}}, (87)

where we made use of the separability of the Born distributions, and of the integrator f⁡(x,y)=fx​(x)​fy​(y)f(x,y)=f_{x}(x)f_{y}(y) which we have observed in Section 3.

Appendix F Machine precision on small systems, the limitation of Monte Carlo sampling, and the importance of curvature

We now demonstrate the theoretical possibility of solving infidelity-based optimizations to machine precision. Specifically, we revisit the quench dynamics studied in Section 4.2, involving a quench from h=∞h=\infty to h=hc/10h=h_{c}/10, but now on a smaller 4×44\times 4 lattice—small enough to allow exact summation over the entire Hilbert space.

In Fig. 10(a-b), we show the variational p-tVMC dynamics computed by evaluating all statistical averages relevant to the optimization exactly. These results exhibit perfect agreement with the exact solution, with optimizations converging to the target state within machine precision.

By contrast, performing the same simulations using Monte Carlo sampling—i.e., evaluating statistical averages over a finite number of samples—yields results similar to those shown in Section 4.1. While convergence remains qualitatively good, it no longer reaches machine precision. As discussed in Section 3.3.1, this discrepancy is likely due to poor estimation of the gradient and curvature matrix when using limited sample sizes, which leads to unreliable updates. Indeed, increasing the number of samples steadily improves the results, bringing them closer to the exact, noiseless solution. Achieving results comparable to full-summation, however, appears to require a number of samples on the order of the Hilbert space dimension itself. This is illustrated in Fig. 10(c), where we display optimization trajectories for the following infidelity minimization problem:

θ∗=argmin𝜃​ℐ​(|ψt⟩,|ψθ⟩).\theta^{*}=\underset{\theta}{\operatorname{argmin}}\,\,\mathcal{I}(\ket{\psi_{t}},\ket{\psi_{\theta}}). (88)

The initial parameter configuration corresponds to the state at time J​t=1.25Jt=1.25, obtained from the noiseless p-tVMC simulation shown in Fig. 10(a-b). The target state |ψt⟩\ket{\psi_{t}} at time J​t=1.3Jt=1.3, by contrast, is taken from the exact evolution of the TFIM dynamics and encoded exactly, using one complex-valued parameter per entry of the state vector.

We now use this simple toy problem to provide a clear illustration of the importance of incorporating curvature information into the optimization strategy to ensure reliable convergence. To isolate the effect of the optimization method from other sources of error—such as Monte Carlo noise and model expressivity—we consider an idealized setting in which all statistical averages required to compute the objective’s gradient and curvature matrix are evaluated exactly by summing over the entire Hilbert space at each optimization step. Moreover, as shown in Fig. 10, the chosen CNN model with 𝚯CNN=(10,10,10,10,3)\bm{\Theta}_{\mathrm{CNN}}=(10,10,10,10;3) is able to represent the target state at time J​t=1.3Jt=1.3 with machine precision accuracy. In Fig. 11, we compare the performance of NGD and Adam on the same state-compression task studied in Fig. 10(c). The results show that Adam converges significantly more slowly and often becomes trapped in local minima, failing to accurately compress the target state. By contrast, NGD achieves rapid and reliable convergence. To further explore the role of curvature information, we modulate the damping parameter λ\lambda, which interpolates between NGD and standard gradient descent. For large values of λ\lambda, the curvature information is heavily suppressed by regularization, and the behavior approaches that of vanilla gradient descent or Adam. As λ\lambda is decreased, curvature plays a more prominent role in shaping the optimization path, culminating in exponential convergence for λ=10−4\lambda=10^{-4}. Overall, this toy problem highlights the critical role of NGD in learning large, global transformations of the quantum state, especially in regimes where precise convergence is required.

Appendix G Exact application of diagonal operators

Let |ψθ⟩=∑xψθ​(x)​|x⟩\ket{\psi_{\theta}}=\sum_{x}\psi_{\theta}(x)\ket{x} be a variational state and A^=∑x,yAx​y​|x⟩⟨y|\hat{A}=\sum_{x,y}A_{xy}\outerproduct{x}{y} a generic operator acting on it. We want to find a way to reduce the application of A^\hat{A} on |ψθ⟩\ket{\psi_{\theta}} to a change of parameters θ→θ′\theta\to\theta^{\prime}. In other words, we want to find θ′\theta^{\prime} such that

|ψθ′⟩=A^​|ψθ⟩.\ket{\psi_{\theta'}}=\hat{A}\ket{\psi_{\theta}}. (89)

If successful, this procedure would allow us to apply A^\hat{A} on |ψθ⟩\ket{\psi_{\theta}} exactly and at no computational expense. Unfortunately, for a generic parametrization of the state, or a generic operator, this is not possible. The problem greatly simplifies if we restrict to diagonal operators of the form A^=∑xAx​|x⟩⟨x|\hat{A}=\sum_{x}A_{x}\outerproduct{x}{x}, whose application on a generic variational state reads A^​|ψθ⟩=∑xAx​ψθ​(x)​|x⟩\hat{A}\ket{\psi_{\theta}}=\sum_{x}A_{x}\psi_{\theta}(x)\ket{x}. Even in this simple case, the transformation θ→θ′\theta\to\theta^{\prime} satisfying |ψθ′⟩=A^​|ψθ⟩\ket{\psi_{\theta'}}=\hat{A}\ket{\psi_{\theta}} is not guaranteed to exist. Consider, however, the improved ansatz |ψθ,ϕ⟩=∑xψθ,ϕ​(x)​|x⟩\ket{\psi_{\theta,\phi}}=\sum_{x}\psi_{\theta,\phi}(x)\ket{x} where

ψθ,ϕ​(x)=(Ax)ϕ​ψθ​(x)withϕ∈ℂ.\psi_{\theta,\phi}(x)=(A_{x})^{\phi}\psi_{\theta}(x)\quad\text{with}\quad\phi\in\mathbb{C}. (90)

The application of A^\hat{A} on this state reads

A^​|ψθ,ϕ⟩=∑xAx​ψθ,ϕ​(x)​|x⟩=∑x(Ax)ϕ+1​ψθ​(x)​|x⟩=|ψθ,ϕ+1⟩\hat{A}\ket{\psi_{\theta,\phi}}=\sum_{x}A_{x}\psi_{\theta,\phi}(x)\ket{x}=\sum_{x}(A_{x})^{\phi+1}\psi_{\theta}(x)\ket{x}=\ket{\psi_{\theta,\phi+1}} (91)

The action of A^\hat{A} on |ψθ,ϕ⟩\ket{\psi_{\theta,\phi}} can thus be exactly reduced to the parameter transformation (θ,ϕ)→(θ,ϕ+1)(\theta,\phi)\to(\theta,\phi+1) which can be computed at virtually no computational expense. Note that while the additional multiplicative layer has a structure determined by A^\hat{A}, the network ψθ​(x)\psi_{\theta}(x) to which this layer is added is completely arbitrary.

This procedure can be easily generalized to multiple diagonal operations which, of course, commute with each other. Given A^=∑xAx​|x⟩⟨x|\hat{A}=\sum_{x}A_{x}\outerproduct{x}{x} and B^=∑xBx​|x⟩⟨x|\hat{B}=\sum_{x}B_{x}\outerproduct{x}{x}, we define the improved ansatz as

ψθ,ϕA,ϕB​(x)=(Bx)ϕB​(Ax)ϕA​ψθ​(x).\psi_{\theta,\phi_{A},\phi_{B}}(x)=(B_{x})^{\phi_{B}}(A_{x})^{\phi_{A}}\psi_{\theta}(x). (92)

The application of A^\hat{A} without B^\hat{B} is equivalent to (θ,ϕA,ϕB)→(θ,ϕA+1,ϕB)(\theta,\phi_{A},\phi_{B})\to(\theta,\phi_{A}+1,\phi_{B}). The application of B^\hat{B} without A^\hat{A} is equivalent to (θ,ϕA,ϕB)→(θ,ϕA,ϕB+1)(\theta,\phi_{A},\phi_{B})\to(\theta,\phi_{A},\phi_{B}+1). The simultaneous application of A^\hat{A} and B^\hat{B} is equivalent to the transformation (θ,ϕA,ϕB)→(θ,ϕA+1,ϕB+1)(\theta,\phi_{A},\phi_{B})\to(\theta,\phi_{A}+1,\phi_{B}+1). Note that we never act on the network itself (θ\theta is never changed).

G.1 Z​ZZZ-operations

Let |ψθ⟩\ket{\psi_{\theta}} be an arbitrary ansatz for the state of a system of NN spin-1/21/2 particles, and

A^=exp⁡(α​σ^μz​σ^νz)=∑xeα​xμ​xν​|x⟩⟨x|≡∑xAx​|x⟩⟨x|withμ,ν∈[1,…,N].\hat{A}=\exp{\alpha\sz_\mu\sz_\nu}=\sum_{x}e^{\,\alpha\,x_{\mu}x_{\nu}}\outerproduct{x}{x}\equiv\sum_{x}A_{x}\outerproduct{x}{x}\quad\text{with}\quad\mu,\nu\in[1,\ldots,N]. (93)

the Z​ZZZ-operation acting on spins μ\mu and ν\nu. To encode the action of A^\hat{A} as a change of parameters we define the improved ansatz

ψθ,ϕ​(x)=(Ax)ϕ​ψθ​(x)=eα​ϕ​xμ​xν​ψθ​(x)≡eϕ​xμ​xν​ψθ​(x),\psi_{\theta,\phi}(x)=(A_{x})^{\phi}\psi_{\theta}(x)=e^{\,\alpha\phi\,x_{\mu}x_{\nu}}\psi_{\theta}(x)\equiv e^{\,\phi\,x_{\mu}x_{\nu}}\psi_{\theta}(x), (94)

where, in the last equality, we absorb α\alpha in the parameter ϕ\phi without loss of generality. As expected, |ψθ,ϕ⟩→A^​|ψθ,ϕ⟩≡(θ,ϕ)→(θ,ϕ+1)\ket{\psi_{\theta,\phi}}\to\hat{A}\ket{\psi_{\theta,\phi}}\equiv(\theta,\phi)\to(\theta,\phi+1). This ansatz accounts for the application of Z​ZZZ-operations on a fixed pair of spins, namely spin μ\mu and ν\nu. For this reason the additional parameter ϕ\phi is a scalar. In general, however, we want to reserve the right to apply the operation between any pair of spins and/or on multiple pairs simultaneously.

Consider now the application of Z​ZZZ-rotations on two pairs of spins: (μ,ν\mu,\nu) and (μ′,ν′\mu^{\prime},\nu^{\prime}). Said differently, we want to find an ansatz to incorporate the action of A^=exp⁡(αμ​ν​σ^μz​σ^νz)\hat{A}=\exp{\alpha_{\mu\nu} \sz_\mu\sz_\nu}, of B^=exp⁡(αμ′​ν′​σ^μ′z​σ^ν′z)\hat{B}=\exp{\alpha_{\mu'\nu'} \sz_{\mu'}\sz_{\nu'}}, and of their product A​BAB, as a simple change of parameters 66 6 Here αμ​ν∈ℂ\alpha_{\mu\nu}\in\mathbb{C} is the phase of the gate operation acting on the pair (μ,ν\mu,\nu).. To do so we can incorporate the single-operator ansatz from Eq. 94 into the two-operator structure in Eq. 92 as

ψθ,ϕ​(x)=(Bx)ϕμ′​ν′​(Ax)ϕμ​ν​ψθ​(x)=exp⁡(xμ​ϕμ​ν​xν)​exp⁡(xμ′​ϕμ′​ν′​xν′)​ψθ​(x)=exp⁡(xμ​ϕμ​ν​xν+xμ′​ϕμ′​ν′​xν′)​ψθ​(x).\psi_{\theta,\bm{\phi}}(x)=(B_{x})^{\phi_{\mu^{\prime}\nu^{\prime}}}(A_{x})^{\phi_{\mu\nu}}\psi_{\theta}(x)=\exp{x_\mu\phi_{\mu\nu} x_\nu}\exp{x_{\mu'} \phi_{\mu'\nu'} x_{\nu'}}\psi_{\theta}(x)=\exp{x_\mu\phi_{\mu\nu} x_\nu+ x_{\mu'} \phi_{\mu'\nu'} x_{\nu'}}\psi_{\theta}(x). (95)

Note that now ϕ=(ϕμ​ν,ϕμ′​ν′)\bm{\phi}=(\phi_{\mu\nu},\phi_{\mu^{\prime}\nu^{\prime}}) is a two-dimensional vector. This can be further generalized to account for Z​ZZZ-operations between any two spins via the ansatz

ψθ,ϕ​(x)=exp⁡{∑i​jxi​ϕi​j​xj}​ψθ​(x)=exp⁡(𝒙​ϕ​𝒙⊤)​ψθ​(x).\psi_{\theta,\bm{\phi}}(x)=\operatorname{exp}\Big\{\sum_{ij}x_{i}\phi_{ij}x_{j}\Big\}\psi_{\theta}(x)=\exp{\bm x\bm\phi\bm x^\top}\psi_{\theta}(x). (96)

Note that the multiplicative layer added to the network is exactly a two-body Jastrow ansatz where ϕ=[ϕμ​ν]\bm{\phi}=[\phi_{\mu\nu}] is an N×NN\times N matrix. Application of the operator A^μ​ν=exp⁡(αμ​ν​σ^μz​σ^νz)\hat{A}_{\mu\nu}=\exp{\alpha_{\mu\nu} \sz_\mu\sz_\nu} is equivalent to the parameter transformation ϕμ​ν→ϕμ​ν+αμ​ν\phi_{\mu\nu}\to\phi_{\mu\nu}+\alpha_{\mu\nu}. In general we parameterize the log-amplitude of the wave function log⁡ψθ,ϕ​(x)=𝒙​ϕ​𝒙⊤+log⁡ψθ​(x)\log\psi_{\theta,\bm{\phi}}(x)=\bm{x}\bm{\phi}\bm{x}^{\top}+\log\psi_{\theta}(x), so that the multiplicative layer actually becomes an additive one.

Appendix H Neural network architectures

In this section we review the two architectures used in this work.

H.1 Convolutional neural networks

Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are particularly well-suited for processing and analyzing grid-like data, such as images or quantum systems on a lattice. The architecture of a CNN consists of multiple layers indexed by ℓ∈[1,NL]\ell\in[1,N_{L}], typically structured as alternating non-linear and affine transformations. For a system defined on a square lattice of linear length LL and number of particles N=L2N=L^{2}, the input layer (ℓ=1\ell=1) receives the configuration vector x=(s1,…,sN)x=(s_{1},\ldots,s_{N}), which is reshaped into an L×LL\times L matrix as X=vec−1⁡(x)X=\operatorname{vec}^{-1}(x), where vec\operatorname{vec} represents the vectorization operation [110].

The building block of CNNs is the convolutional layer, where filters (or kernels) are applied to local regions of the input, learning spatial hierarchies of features. This is analogous to performing convolution operations over a lattice, capturing local correlations across the system. Let the output of the ℓ\ell-th layer be

X(ℓ)=[X(ℓ)]i,jα∈ℂCℓ⊗ℂHℓ×Wℓwith{i∈[0,Hℓ−1],j∈[0,Wℓ−1],α∈[0,Cℓ−1]X^{(\ell)}=[X^{(\ell)}]^{\alpha}_{i,j}\in\mathbb{C}^{C_{\ell}}\otimes\mathbb{C}^{H_{\ell}\times W_{\ell}}\quad\mbox{with}\quad\begin{cases}i\,\in[0,H_{\ell}-1],\\ j\,\in[0,W_{\ell}-1],\\ \alpha\in[0,C_{\ell}-1]\end{cases} (97)

where (Hℓ,Wℓ)(H_{\ell},W_{\ell}) are the height and width of the processed data at layer step ℓ\ell, and CℓC_{\ell} is the number of channels. The convolution operation yielding the data structure of the (ℓ+1)(\ell+1)-th layer is

(X(ℓ+1))m,nβ=σℓ​([X(ℓ)⊛F(ℓ)]m,nβ)=σℓ​(∑α∑i,j[F(ℓ)]i,jα​β​[X(ℓ)]m+i,n+jα)with{i∈[0,hℓ−1],j∈[0,wℓ−1],β∈[0,cℓ−1]\quantity(X^{(\ell+1)})^{\beta}_{m,n}=\sigma_{\ell}\quantity( \bigl[X^{(\ell)} \circledast F^{(\ell)}\bigr]^{\beta}_{m,n})=\sigma_{\ell}\quantity(\sum_{\alpha} \sum_{i,j} \bigl[F^{(\ell)}\bigr]_{i,j}^{\alpha\beta}\,\bigl[X^{(\ell)}\bigr]_{m+i,\, n+j}^{\alpha} )\quad\mbox{with}\quad\begin{cases}i\,\in[0,h_{\ell}-1],\\ j\,\in[0,w_{\ell}-1],\\ \beta\in[0,c_{\ell}-1]\end{cases} (98)

where σℓ\sigma_{\ell} is the activation function, (hℓ,wℓ)(h_{\ell},w_{\ell}) is the size of the convolutional kernel F(ℓ)F^{(\ell)}, and cℓc_{\ell} is its output dimension.

For the activation functions, we follow the approach in Ref. [49]. The activation function in the first layer conists of the first three non-vanishing terms of the series expansion of logcosh⁡(z)\operatorname{logcosh}(z), ensuring the incorporation of the system’s ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} symmetry in the absence of bias in the first layer. It is defined as

σ1​(z)=z22−z412+z645.\sigma_{1}(z)=\frac{z^{2}}{2}-\frac{z^{4}}{12}+\frac{z^{6}}{45}. (99)

In subsequent layers, its derivative is used

σℓ>1​(z)=z2−z33+215​z5.\sigma_{\ell>1}(z)=\frac{z}{2}-\frac{z^{3}}{3}+\frac{2}{15}z^{5}. (100)

We use circular padding to respect periodic boundary conditions, ensuring moreover that the spatial dimensions remain constant across layers, Hℓ=Wℓ=LH_{\ell}=W_{\ell}=L. Both dilation and stride are set to one across all layers, and a fixed kernel size hℓ=wℓ=kh_{\ell}=w_{\ell}=k is used. A final dense layer is used to pool the output of the CNN into a scalar output. After the convolutional layers, a fully connected layer reduces the output of the convolutional sequence to a scalar.

The CNN structure can is summarized by a tuple 𝚯CNN=(c1,…,cNL,k)\bm{\Theta}_{\rm CNN}=(c_{1},\ldots,c_{N_{L}};k), where cℓc_{\ell} represents the number of channels in each layer, and kk denotes the kernel size. A sketch of the architecture is shown in Fig. 13.

H.2 Vision Transformer

The Vision Transformer (ViT) is a state-of-the-art architecture in machine learning. While originally developed for image classification and segmentation, it has recently been adopted as a powerful ansatz for quantum many-body wavefunctions [39, 96]. Below, we describe the key components and parameters of this architecture as applied to NQS. For a spin-1/21/2 system defined on a square lattice of linear length LL, the input consists of a configuration vector 𝒙=(s1,…,sN){\bm{x}}=(s_{1},\ldots,s_{N}) with si∈{±1}s_{i}\in\{\pm 1\}. This vector is reshaped into an L×LL\times L matrix 𝑿=vec−1⁡(𝒙)\bm{X}=\operatorname{vec}^{-1}({\bm{x}}), with vec\operatorname{vec} representing the vectorization operation [110]. This matrix corresponds to a specific configuration of spins on the lattice.

Patch Extraction and Embedding.

The matrix is divided into n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} non-overlapping patches of size b×bb\times b, namely 𝑿1,…,𝑿n\bm{X}_{1},\ldots,\bm{X}_{n} with 𝑿i∈{±1}b×b\bm{X}_{i}\in\{\pm 1\}^{b\times b}. Of course, for this to be possible, the total number of sites must be an integer multiple of bb. Each patch is flattened, and linearly projected into a high-dimensional embedding space of dimension dd. This transforms the spin values into a vector representation that is processed by the encoder blocks:

{𝑿i∈{±1}b×b}i=1n→{vec(𝑿i)∈{±1}b2}i=1n→{𝒙i∈ℝd}i=1n.\bigl\{\bm{X}_{i}\in\{\pm 1\}^{b\times b}\bigr\}_{i=1}^{n}\,\,\to\,\,\bigl\{\operatorname{vec}(\bm{X}_{i})\in\{\pm 1\}^{b^{2}}\bigl\}_{i=1}^{n}\,\,\to\,\,\bigl\{{\bm{x}}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\bigl\}_{i=1}^{n}. (101)
Encoder Blocks.

The core of the ViT architecture consists of NLN_{L} encoder blocks. The input to each block is a set of nn vectors {𝒙i(ℓ)∈ℝd}i=1n\bigl\{{\bm{x}}_{i}^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\bigl\}_{i=1}^{n} with ℓ=1,…,NL\ell=1,\ldots,N_{L} and 𝒙i(1)=𝒙i{\bm{x}}_{i}^{(1)}=\bm{x}_{i}. Each encoder block correlates the input vectors thereby capturing long-range correlations and intricate interactions in the quantum system. Each block consists of the following components:

Multi-Head Factored Attention Mechanism.

The generic self-attention mechanism is defined by three rectangular matrices of parameters 𝑸,𝑲,𝑽\bm{Q},\bm{K},\bm{V} known as Query, Key, and Value. For each of the nn input vectors 𝒙i\bm{x}_{i}, three new vectors are computed: 𝒒i=𝑸​𝒙i\bm{q}_{i}=\bm{Q}{\bm{x}}_{i}, 𝒌i=𝑲​𝒙i\bm{k}_{i}=\bm{K}{\bm{x}}_{i}, 𝒗i=𝑽​𝒙i\bm{v}_{i}=\bm{V}{\bm{x}}_{i}. These vectors are then combined with one another to create nn attention vectors 𝑨i=∑j=1nα⁡(𝒒i,𝒌j)​𝒗j\bm{A}_{i}=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\alpha(\bm{q}_{i},\bm{k}_{j})\,\bm{v}_{j} where the attention weights α⁡(𝒒i,𝒌j)\alpha(\bm{q}_{i},\bm{k}_{j}) modulate the contribution of each value vector 𝒗j\bm{v}_{j} to the globally mixed vector 𝑨i\bm{A}_{i}. To improve the performance of the model, a multi-head attention mechanism is often preferred to this self-attention. In this case, a set of h∈ℕh\in\mathbb{N} matrices {𝑸μ,𝑲μ,𝑽μ}μ=1h\{\bm{Q}^{\mu},\bm{K}^{\mu},\bm{V}^{\mu}\}_{\mu=1}^{h} are used to compute in parallel a set of hh sets of nn self-attention vectors {𝑨1μ,…,𝑨nμ}μ=1h\{\bm{A}_{1}^{\mu},\ldots,\bm{A}_{n}^{\mu}\}_{\mu=1}^{h} with 𝑨iμ∈ℝr\bm{A}_{i}^{\mu}\in\mathbb{R}^{r} and r=d/hr=d/h. While in general we would have

𝑨iμ=∑j=1nα⁡(𝑸​𝒙iμ,𝑲​𝒙jμ)​𝑽​𝒙j,\bm{A}_{i}^{\mu}=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\alpha(\bm{Q}{\bm{x}}_{i}^{\mu},\bm{K}{\bm{x}}_{j}^{\mu})\,\bm{V}{\bm{x}}_{j}, (102)

the simplification proposed in [96, 39] takes

𝑨iμ=∑j=1nαi​jμ​𝑽μ​𝒙j,\bm{A}_{i}^{\mu}=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\alpha_{ij}^{\mu}\,\bm{V}^{\mu}{\bm{x}}_{j}, (103)

where 𝑽μ\bm{V}^{\mu} is an r×dr\times d matrix and αi​jμ\alpha_{ij}^{\mu} is a tensor of parameters depending on the positions of groups of spins (patches i,ji,j) and independent instead of the actual spin configuration at those positions (no dependence on 𝒙i{\bm{x}}_{i} or 𝒙j\bm{x}_{j}). To summarize:

{𝒙i∈ℝd}i=1,…,n→{𝑨iμ∈ℝr}i=1,…,nμ=1,…,h.\bigl\{{\bm{x}}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\bigr\}_{i=1,\ldots,n}\,\,\to\,\,\{\bm{A}_{i}^{\mu}\in\mathbb{R}^{r}\}_{\begin{subarray}{c}i=1,\ldots,n\\ \mu=1,\ldots,h\end{subarray}}. (104)
Feed-Forward Neural Network.

The hh sets of vectors from the attention layer 𝑨iμ\bm{A}_{i}^{\mu} are first concatenated into a set of nn d-dimensional vectors {𝒚i}i=1n\{\bm{y}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n} with

𝒚i=Concat⁡(𝑨i1,…,𝑨ih)∈ℝd.\bm{y}_{i}=\operatorname{Concat}(\bm{A}^{1}_{i},\ldots,\bm{A}^{h}_{i})\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. (105)

A feed-forward network (FFN) is finally used to process these vectors independently. The hidden layer in this FFN has a dimensionality of nu​p​dn_{\mathrm{u}p}\,d with nupn_{\rm up} the upscaling factor. A GeLU (Gaussian Error Linear Unit) activation function is used between the layers of the FFN, introducing a non-linearity that helps the model capture more complex features. The output of the encoder block is a set of nn vectors

𝒙i(ℓ+1)=FFN⁡(𝒚i)∈ℝnu​p​d.{\bm{x}}^{(\ell+1)}_{i}=\operatorname{FFN}(\bm{y}_{i})\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{\mathrm{u}p}\,d}. (106)

This output is then used as the input to the subsequent block.

Skip Connections and Layer Normalization.

Skip connections are applied across the attention and FFN layers. These connections help alleviate the vanishing gradient problem, allowing the model to train deeper architectures. Layer normalization is applied before both the attention and FFN layers to stabilize the training process and improve convergence.

Output and Wave Function Representation.

After the spin configurations pass through the encoder blocks, the output vectors corresponding to each patch are summed to create a final hidden representation vector

𝒛=∑i=1n𝒙i(NL+1).\bm{z}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\bm{x}_{i}^{(N_{L}+1)}. (107)

This vector represents the configuration in a high-dimensional space and is passed through a final complex-valued fully connected neural network yielding the log-amplitude of our variational wave function:

log⁡ψθ​(𝒙)=∑α=1Klogcosh⁡(bα+𝒘α⋅𝒛),\log\psi_{\theta}({\bm{x}})=\sum_{\alpha=1}^{K}\operatorname{logcosh}(b_{\alpha}+\bm{w}_{\alpha}\cdot\bm{z}), (108)

where 𝑾={bα,𝒘α}α=1K\bm{W}=\{b_{\alpha},\bm{w}_{\alpha}\}_{\alpha=1}^{K} are complex-valued parameters so that {Re(𝑾),Im(𝑾)}⊂θ\{\real(\bm{W}),\imaginary(\bm{W})\}\subset\theta.

We summarize the ViT configuration with the tuple ΘViT=(b,h,r,nup,NL)\Theta_{\mathrm{ViT}}=(b,h,r,n_{\rm up};N_{L}). A schematic representation is shown in Fig. 13.
